top.title: Valkyries parade wasn't just about sports. It was a celebration of who we are. All of us
top.description: Golden State Valkyries' Gabby Williams, center, celebrates with fans along the The Embarcadero during the team's WNBA Championship parade in San Francisco, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle) Did anyone go to school? Did anyone go to work? Did anyone stop smiling? It sure didn't feel like it on a sun-splashed, joyous Wednesday afternoon, when the Bay Area showed up and showed out for their newest champions, their newest local icons. The Golden State Valkyries championship parade, like almost everything the team has done in its brief lifetime, felt flawless, unique and perfectly Bay Area. A uniting, inclusive, delightful bolt of energy. The event was a mashup of an impromptu holiday, Pride parade, women's empowerment festival, Too Short concert, Blue Wave bash and - oh yeah - a sports title celebration. "It's like a movie," said Peter Guber, the team's part owner and a successful film producer. He was looking out over a cinematic scene, as the Valkyries ferry boat pulled out of the port at Jack London Square, and began the trip from Oakland to San Francisco across the sparkling bay waters. Iconic setting. Legendary characters. Spectacular story. Everything about this team has been intentional, well thought out, from the start. And the victory celebration was no exception. It united all our disparate parts, our proud identities, our different cities. It highlighted what is uniquely us . And the day after much of the nation rejected the current regime's divisive agenda, it was a feel-good, validating celebration. Though most in the throngs that lined the Embarcadero parade route were far too young to have any memory of the 49ers first Super Bowl championship, this Valkyries team has brought a similar feeling to the Bay Area. The 49ers helped bring San Francisco out of a very dark space, created by the Milk-Moscone murders at City Hall, the Jonestown tragedy in Guyana and somber days of a debilitating recession. Joe Montana and Ronnie Lott soothed the city's soul, made people proud to say they were from San Francisco. The Valkyries were born when the city was still being vilified by conservative pundits, struggling to recover from the pandemic, serving as a national punchline. Their two years of existence have coincided with the Trump administration's vicious attacks on the LGBTQ+ community, other marginalized groups and on women's rights. Which is why their victory party wasn't just about sports. It was a celebration of who we are. All of us. And particularly a celebration of women. This was our first sports party for a professional women's team, representing the half of society shut out of sports for too long. One that used love and friendship and the fight for equity as keys to victory. This is the first women's professional team to stand on the mountaintop with the Bay Area's other sports icons. top.description: Minnesota Vikings wide receiver Jauan Jennings (14) runs after a catch against the Indianapolis Colts in the fourth quarter on Oct. 25 in Minneapolis. (Bruce Kluckhohn/Associated Press) When head coach Kyle Shanahan was asked Wednesday about Vikings wide receiver Jauan Jennings reportedly declining a trade last week that would have sent him back to the San Francisco 49er s, Shanahan said the story didn't capture the full picture. "The report was accurate," he said, "just not totally exactly detailed up." What does that mean? Well, the part of the report from Fox's Jay Glazer that included how Jennings declined to get on a FaceTime call with Shanahan and general manager John Lynch , who were hoping to seal the deal? That was wrong, Shanahan said. Or, rather, not totally exactly detailed up. "It was actually - it was J.J. FaceTiming me," Shanahan said. "… It was a good talk, but he's with good people (in Minnesota). He likes where he's at. And I thought it made sense what he said and I agreed with him." That doesn't make total sense. Jennings has six catches on 10 targets in six games with a 6-1 team that values him so little that it's willing to trade him to a 6-1 team it could be battling for the NFC's No. 1 seed. And he's enjoying that situation so much that he declined a trade to his employer for his first six NFL seasons (2020-2025) that clearly still values him? It sounds like there's more to the story, possibly having to do with the 49ers not meeting Jennings' contract extension demands last year. Whatever the case, here's what the story - warts and all - tells us: The 49ers are in the market for a wide receiver before the NFL's trade deadline on Tuesday. Shanahan spoke Wednesday for the first time since the 49ers traded for Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner during last week's bye and said the 49ers might not be done dealing. His message contrasted with last year's when he downplayed deadline activity. At the deadline, the 49ers were 6-3, but had lost two All-Pros, pass rusher Nick Bosa and linebacker Fred Warner , to season-ending injuries. They made a low-wattage move, acquiring pass rusher Keion White from the Patriots in a swap of late-round picks. "I do know our team's better than it was last year," Shanahan said. top.title: Spurs fashion gets hairy as Keldon Johnson's mustache steals the show
top.description: Keldon Johnson arrives at the Frost Bank Center ahead of the matchup against the Dallas Mavericks. (Courtesy of San Antonio Spurs) Camouflage, flashy kicks and a mustache that deserves its own starting lineup. The San Antonio Spurs brought plenty of personality to the Frost Bank Center on Wednesday night, Nov. 4, ahead of their showdown with the Dallas Mavericks. From designer sneakers to statement graphic tees, the Silver and Black made sure their pregame fashion was anything but ordinary. Here's a closer look at what five Spurs players wore before tipoff. Forget wearing flashy clothes, Keldon Johnson's mustache might have been the biggest fashion statement of the night. The reigning Sixth Man of the Year arrived sporting a playful mustache that looked straight out of a 1970s detective show, giving his pregame appearance a little extra character. Johnson wore a white VALE FOREVER "Air Donald" graphic tee featuring Ronald McDonald soaring toward a basketball hoop, layered beneath a light-gray zip-up hoodie. He paired the outfit with blue jeans, Bottega Veneta Orbit low-top sneakers, and his signature "KJ" chain. Now, Stephon Castle kicked things off in a Boredom Kills Trust camouflage long-sleeve sweatshirt featuring a large graphic across the chest. The Spurs guard paired the sweatshirt with light-wash blue jeans and a cross necklace, keeping his look casual while letting the camouflage do the talking. It looks like Castle's "Area 51" teammate, Victor Wembanyama, also got the camouflage memo. At 7-foot-4, blending into a crowd isn't exactly Wembanyama's specialty, but the Spurs superstar gave it a shot Wednesday night, wearing a black zip-up hoodie layered beneath a Nike Tech Dri-FIT Woven Camo Windrunner Oversized Jacket in Neutral Olive and Black. He completed the look with gray Nike joggers and olive-green Nike sneakers, keeping things comfortable with an outdoors-inspired ensemble. With his hood up and hands tucked into his pockets, Wembanyama looked ready for a covert mission rather than an NBA matchup. Spurs guard Dylan Harper kept things coordinated in a forest-green Nike hoodie and matching sweatpants layered over a black T-shirt. He completed the outfit with black Nike sneakers and his signature diamond-encrusted No. 2 chain, adding some sparkle to his otherwise understated look. Between laid-back camouflage fits and colorful sweats, Johnson personality stands out the most as the Spurs get ready to face their in-state rival, the Dallas Mavericks. top.title: Cheboygan volleyball to face Kingsley in D2 district title match
top.description: GRAYLING — Cheboygan volleyball is back in the district final. Playing in an MHSAA Division 2 district semifinal clash on Wednesday, Nov. 4, the Chiefs kept their season alive by capturing a 3-0 victory at Grayling (25-23, 25-23, 25-23). CHEBOYGAN JV VOLLEYBALL FINISHES 41-0: Cheboygan JV volleyball team caps off perfect 41-0 season on court TUESDAY DISTRICT ROUNDUP: Mackinaw City, NMCA advance to MHSAA district volleyball finals DISTRICT VOLLEYBALL PREVIEW: Previewing, predicting Cheboygan-area volleyball district tournaments The Chiefs took a 21-16 lead in the first set after junior Sophia Naden delivered a kill. However, Grayling, which trailed 24-16, rattled off an 8-0 run to tie the set and put all the pressure on the Chiefs. But following a Grayling attacking error, Naden hammered home another kill to give Cheboygan a one-set lead. The Vikings responded impressively by building a 16-12 lead in the second, but the Chiefs countered with a 7-3 spurt that was capped off by a kill from junior Diem Schley, which tied things up at 19. The teams went back and forth during several points, but the Chiefs took the lead for good when another kill from Naden gave Cheboygan a one-point advantage, which was then followed by another point that gave the Chiefs the set and victory. Much like the second set, the Chiefs trailed for much of the third. However, a pivotal run helped them tie the set. Polishing off the Cheboygan win was Schley, whose match-winning kill was too much for Grayling to handle. With the victory, the Chiefs (18-14-4) travel to face Kingsley (47-5-1) in a 6 p.m. district final on Thursday, Nov. 5. The Stags, who won last year's Division 3 state title, swept the Chiefs in Cheboygan earlier this season. Cheboygan fell to Ogemaw Heights in a D2 district final last year. top.title: How much Cleveland magic can pitching coach Joe Torres bring to Reds?
top.description: The Cincinnati Reds’ new pitching coach goes from one of the best pitching-developmental organizations of the past few decades to one of the worst-performing pitching staffs of the 2026 season. Now all he has to do is bring enough secret pitching sauce from Cleveland in his first year as a lead pitching coach to fix a Reds staff that needs to become one of the top staffs in the league again – without All-Star Hunter Greene – for the Reds to have any chance to compete in 2027. Reds Hall of Fame Piniella Baker Pair of former Reds managers on Hall of Fame ballot Welcome to Cincinnati, Joe Torres. Torres, 44, was hired by the Reds this week to replace Derek Johnson after spending the past five seasons as an assistant to highly regarded Carl Willis in Cleveland, where he worked under Reds manager Terry Francona for two of those seasons and where the Guardians’ pitching staff ranked among the top 10 in the majors all five years. “This being my first year in this lead position and having a manager with the experience that Tito has, that’s so comforting for me,” said Torres, who has less than four weeks to get to know a group of pitchers he has only seen from across the field before MLB owners impose an industry shutdown Dec. 1 with a widely anticipated labor lockout. “I’ve got a small time window here with getting to know guys,” Torres said on the day his hiring was announced, Nov. 4. “It’s getting to know them as a person first. I’ve got to get in there and see what makes them tick, what motivates them, and see where I can help them and help add value.” Injuries and underperformance – especially when it came to issuing walks and hitting guys – buried the pitching staff in 2026 and by extension the Reds chances to compete during a 75-87, last-place season. “We have got to work ahead (in the count),” Francona said during an interview later in the day on WLW-radio. “There were so many innings last year when even when we got through the inning there were a bunch of 3-2 counts (and high pitch totals). That’s not going to work out over the course of a game or the season. We’ve got to be more economical.” Reds pitchers led the majors in walks and were fourth in hit batters. Torres called that a “priority” and plans to start breaking down solutions as he gets to know his pitchers. “I’ve got to get in and see why (that happened). top.title: ‘Inexcusable and Semi-Reprehensible,’ ‘You’re Ruining Your Players’ — Bill Simmons Rips Adam Silver’s ‘Negligence and Greed’ Over 82-Game Schedule
top.description: ‘Inexcusable and Semi-Reprehensible,’ ‘You’re Ruining Your Players’ — Bill Simmons Rips Adam Silver’s ‘Negligence and Greed’ Over 82-Game Schedule Bill Simmons wants the NBA to cut its regular season from 82 games to 70, and he blames Commissioner Adam Silver and the league’s owners for the current schedule. The Ringer founder made his case on Tuesday’s episode of “The Bill Simmons Podcast.” His argument also centered on potential expansion in Las Vegas and Seattle, which could bring billions in fees to the league’s current owners. Bill Simmons Targets Adam Silver Over NBA Schedule and Potential Expansion Fees The podcaster opened his criticism by directing it at the league office. “Listen, I don’t know how many times I’ve talked about this on the pod about the schedule and about how this, to me, is just inexcusable and semi-reprehensible that whoever is in charge of the league, which I think is Adam Silver these days, that he doesn’t care,” Simmons said . The NBA has maintained an 82-game regular season since 1967-68, apart from seasons shortened by labor disputes or other disruptions. He continued, “You’re ruining your players … and you’re hurting careers, and you’re shortening careers. This should be a 70-game season. And if you talk to literally everybody who plays basketball, all of them would say the season needs to be shorter. And if you don’t do it at this point, I just think it’s negligent. I really do. I think it’s actual negligence and greed.” The NBA has 30 franchises, and adding teams in Las Vegas and Seattle would mark its first expansion since the Charlotte Bobcats joined the league in 2004. That potential expansion is central to Simmons’ argument because of the money he expects the league’s current owners to receive. “The question for me is, you’re gonna make all this money … that’s gonna be $9.5 billion for the [Las Vegas] expansion team … They’re gonna get a second thing from Seattle, which is gonna be $7.5 (billion), something like that. … So all these owners are getting, I don’t know, $16 billion in expansion fees,” he said. Those figures are his estimates. In March, the New York Post reported that expansion fees could range from $7 billion to $10 billion per team, with the money going to the NBA’s current owners rather than being shared with players. Cutting 12 games from each team’s schedule would also mean fewer home dates and fewer opportunities to sell tickets and concessions. Simmons questioned why the league would resist cutting games despite that potential windfall. “And yet everyone’s like, ‘Well, we can’t lose games. We’d lose too much money. We’d lose revenue,'” he said. The NBA’s Board of Governors voted March 25 to explore expansion into Las Vegas and Seattle, although neither city has been awarded a franchise. Houston Texans defensive end Will Anderson Jr. had some high praise for Justin Herbert ahead of Sunday’s matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers . However, his assessment of the quarterback’s current play might leave NFL fans wondering what he has been watching. "Herbert, man, he's playing out of his mind." We have a ton of respect for him. We know what to expect a little bit. But Herbert, man, he’s playing out of his mind.” The first part of Anderson’s comments are fine. But the last part of the praise isn’t factually correct at this point in Herbert’s career. The Chargers are 0-7, and Herbert has struggled to find consistency in Mike McDaniel’s offense. He has looked uncomfortable in the scheme and made questionable decisions. He and McDaniel are failing to get the most out of an offense that was expected to take a step forward. Los Angeles now faces another difficult test against a Houston defense that has given Herbert problems in the past. top.title: Rece Davis: CFP rankings show ‘needs to be reimagined’ when bracket expands to 24
top.description: Credit: ESPN If the College Football Playoff rankings show feels like a chore with a 12-team field, just imagine how it will be with 24 teams starting next season. After the heavily criticized first rankings release of the season on ESPN this week, host Rece Davis deftly avoided direct criticism of the selection committee while noting on The Pat McAfee Show that he expected significant turnover among the teams going forward. Davis is tasked with interviewing committee chair Hunter Yurachek about the list each week, and creating some semblance of a track record over the course of the season. In a follow-up conversation Wednesday on The College GameDay Podcast , Davis expressed uncertainty over the future of the rankings show. “If this continues … I don’t know that the show itself continues. I assume it will, because it’s still under the original contract,” he said. “But it will certainly feel different. It felt different when we went to 12 a couple of years ago, it’s certainly going to feel different when we go to 24.” While insider Pete Thamel confirmed that he expects the rankings show will continue under the CFP’s updated agreement with ESPN , Davis acknowledged the show could become very dry running through two-dozen teams. The longtime College GameDay host suggested the show should not air any rankings beyond 25 even once the tournament expands, and offered the idea of perhaps starting with the first team out to build suspense. “It probably needs to be reimagined,” he said. “I mean, are we really going to start … at 35? But then people are like, ‘Let’s go.’ So I think if you start at 25, [it’s], ‘OK here’s the first team out.’ Maybe you do it like that.” The show draws millions of viewers and theoretically helps the CFP selection committee hold itself accountable. However, it has become a source of tension at ESPN and in the industry. Star commentator Kirk Herbstreit bowed out from the broadcast early on , and in-house critics such as Michael Wilbon have railed against the rankings show. When the field doubles in size , ESPN could have a different issue on its hands. The show could simply become too boring or monotonous for fans. nigeria.title: Google turns off AI for schoolchildren by default
nigeria.description: Google has said it will switch off its AI tools for schoolchildren by default, after drawing criticism for pushing artificial intelligence features to students while schools are still debating how the technology should be used in classrooms. The search engine juggernaut dominates technology in American schools. Its education apps, including Gmail, Docs and the Classroom platform, are used in classrooms across the country, and its low-cost Chromebook laptops are the devices US schools most often issue to students. Under the changes Google announced in a blog post on Tuesday, Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Search will be turned off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators switch them on. Google told AFP the new controls would be rolled out worldwide, beginning in the United States, but that it had not yet set a date. The changes also mean schools will not be able to give students Google Search without its AI features. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president for education, told The New York Times that “Search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” as AI features are now built into the company’s search engine. If a school bans AI, he said, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.” New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused Google on X of “trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools.” “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children,” he wrote. More than 150 million students worldwide use Google Classroom, according to a letter Senators Richard Blumenthal and Josh Hawley sent to the company last month asking why AI features had been made the default on school devices. In August, Google opened its Gemini chatbot in Classroom to students of all ages. Students were shown starter prompts tied to their specific class and assignment, offering guided help or study guides, practice quizzes and flashcards built from their course materials. The feature was switched on by default for students at schools that had already enabled Gemini. New York and Los Angeles both announced plans in September to restrict access to AI tools on school devices. “We are reviewing Google’s announcement and its potential implications for schools, educators and students,” a spokesperson for the Los Angeles Unified School District told AFP. The spokesperson said the district believes AI can improve teaching and learning if it is introduced carefully and with clear safeguards, and pointed to district principles requiring that technology support rather than replace teachers and protect student privacy. In a statement on X, Google said Tuesday’s changes give “schools more choice, not less.” “We know there’s concern about students using AI to shortcut schoolwork, and schools have told us they want control,” Google said. nigeria.title: Kekere-Ekun to chair presentation of Pinheiro’s 6 legal publications
nigeria.description: By Innocent Anaba The Chief Justice of Nigeria, CJN, Justice Kudirat Kekere-Ekun, will chair the public presentation of six legal books authored by Dr ‘Kemi Pinheiro, SAN, on November 20, 2026. The publications, which draw on Pinheiro’s nearly four decades of legal practice, examine critical areas of Nigerian law, including criminal litigation, arbitration, corporate insolvency, justice administration and emerging legal issues. The collection comprises Strategies in Criminal Trial: A Practitioner’s Guide; Insolvency Law in Nigeria: Practice and Procedure; Arbitration Law and Practice in Nigeria; Defining Moments: Chronicles of a Silk (Volume One); The Compendium; and MULAN Legal: Trending Issues of Law and Faith – Essays in Honour of ‘Kemi Pinheiro, SAN. The book on criminal trials examines key procedural and evidential issues in criminal proceedings, including the treatment and admissibility of electronic evidence. Similarly, Insolvency Law in Nigeria: Practice and Procedure explores the legal framework governing corporate rescue, restructuring and insolvency proceedings under the Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020. Arbitration Law and Practice in Nigeria examines the country’s arbitration framework, with particular attention to the Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 and the enforcement of arbitral awards. It also addresses the growing importance of alternative dispute resolution in settling commercial disputes. Beyond these practice-oriented publications, Defining Moments: Chronicles of a Silk (Volume One) chronicles Pinheiro’s professional journey and experiences in the legal profession. The Compendium features scholarly essays by legal practitioners and academics, while MULAN Legal: Trending Issues of Law and Faith – Essays in Honour of ‘Kemi Pinheiro, SAN examines the intersection of law, faith and Nigeria’s plural legal system through contributions from various authors. The six publications bring together practical legal guidance, academic research and professional reflections on the development of Nigerian law, with subject matter relevant to judges, legal practitioners, academics and other stakeholders in the administration of justice. The public presentation, organised by Pinheiro LP, is expected to attract members of the judiciary, the Bar, academia and other stakeholders in the legal profession. business.description: Bitcoin Magazine American Bitcoin (ABTC) Posts $126 Million Profit as Holdings Gain $197 Million American Bitcoin Corp. (Nasdaq: ABTC) reported about $126 million in third-quarter net income on Wednesday, a swing from a $57.2 million loss in the prior quarter that rested largely on a $197.3 million gain on the company’s bitcoin holdings rather than on mining revenue. The Miami-based miner and treasury company, a majority-owned subsidiary of Hut 8 Corp. and co-founded with Trump family backing, mined about 891 bitcoin in the quarter at a cost of roughly $42,100 each and ended September with about 8,427 BTC. Mining revenue was about $63.4 million, down from about $67.0 million in the second quarter. Gross profit was about $25.8 million, a 41% margin, compared with about $33.0 million and 49% a quarter earlier, as seasonal power costs rose across its sites. Adjusted EBITDA came in at about $221 million, compared with an Adjusted EBITDA loss of about $45.0 million in the second quarter, according to the company’s release . Eric Trump, co-founder and chief strategy officer of American Bitcoin, said the quarter delivered the net income and Adjusted EBITDA figures while growing the bitcoin reserve and bitcoin per share. Chief Executive Mike Ho said the company kept mining at a structural discount to spot and raised satoshis per share by about 5% without issuing shares through its at-the-market program or buying bitcoin on the open market. A paper gain carried American Bitcoin’s quarter The income statement makes the driver plain. American Bitcoin booked a $197.3 million gain on digital assets in the third quarter, after a $71.2 million loss on that line in the second. Operating income was about $191.8 million. Other expense included a $64.3 million loss on derivatives. Strip the mark-to-market move out of the picture and the operating story looks quieter. Revenue per bitcoin mined was about $71,100, down slightly from about $71,900 in the second quarter, and the cost to mine rose to about $42,100 from about $36,500, the company said. Production of about 891 bitcoin was below the second quarter’s roughly 932 coins, which the company had called its highest quarterly haul on record when it reported a $57.2 million second-quarter loss alongside a climb in holdings to about 8,002 BTC. American Bitcoin said it sold a portion of production to cover operating costs while still adding to its strategic reserve. Holdings rose by about 425 bitcoin, or about 5%, to roughly 8,427 as of Sept. 30. That total includes about 3,090 bitcoin pledged for miner purchases under agreements with Bitmain. Reserve up, satoshis per share up Management’s preferred yardstick is satoshis per share, which rose about 5% to roughly 11,572 from about 10,989 at the end of June. The share count reflects a 1-for-15 reverse stock split effected earlier this year on July 2. The owned fleet stood at about 89,242 bitcoin miners with roughly 28.1 EH/s of capacity at quarter-end. business.title: Judge Lets Stock Perpetual Futures Keep Trading but Says CFTC Likely Overstepped Its Authority
business.description: Bitcoin Magazine Judge Lets Stock Perpetual Futures Keep Trading but Says CFTC Likely Overstepped Its Authority Stock perpetual futures can keep trading on Kalshi, Coinbase Derivatives and Bitnomial for now after a federal judge denied an emergency bid to halt them Tuesday, while finding that the Wall Street-backed challengers are likely to prove the CFTC overstepped its authority. U.S. District Judge Valerie Caproni denied the temporary restraining order on Nov. 3 after a teleconference with the parties, hours after the CFTC said the products could begin trading on U.S.-regulated exchanges. The plaintiff is the Capital Markets Alliance Association, a New York nonprofit whose members include Cboe Global Markets, Citadel Securities and the Healthy Markets Association, according to a declaration from its secretary, Adam Ford. The group sued the CFTC and Chairman Michael S. Selig in the Southern District of New York, case No. 1:26-cv-09608, seeking to undo the approvals of filings by all three exchanges. Caproni wrote that the group “is likely to succeed on the merits” of its claim that the agency lacks statutory authority to allow perpetual derivatives on individual stocks to be offered to retail investors on CFTC-regulated platforms. “Because the perpetual contracts, by definition, do not provide for a ‘sale for future delivery of a single security,’ they cannot be a security future over which the CFTC has statutory and regulatory authority,” she wrote. Instead, she said, the contracts “appear to satisfy the definition of a swap,” which falls to the Securities and Exchange Commission. She also found that the balance of equities and the public interest favor the alliance, writing that the agency’s actions “seem to represent a major disruption to the equities market.” The request failed on one prong. Caproni said the declarations from Cboe, Citadel Securities and Healthy Markets were “conjectural” about the harm members would suffer and did not show irreparable harm that was “actual and imminent.” What the ruling does and does not do The order leaves the approvals in place. It does not decide the case or the alliance’s separate motion for a preliminary injunction. The CFTC’s opposition is due Friday, Nov. 6, and the alliance’s reply is due Tuesday, Nov. 10. The order says that schedule is subject to change by the assigned judge. The docket lists Judge Lorna G. Schofield as assigned to the case. Kalshi was already listing four single-stock perps on Qualcomm, McDonald’s, Amgen and Costco by Wednesday morning, with maximum leverage of 4.9 times. Bloomberg Law reported that the judge signaled she might ultimately side with the Wall Street firms opposed to the products. business.title: French Bank Credit Mutuel Arkea Confirms Cyberattack as ZachXBT Puts Losses Above $133 Million
business.description: Bitcoin Magazine French Bank Credit Mutuel Arkea Confirms Cyberattack as ZachXBT Puts Losses Above $133 Million French bank Credit Mutuel Arkea said Wednesday that a cyberattack allowed hackers to carry out fraudulent transfers from the bank’s own account, a theft that on-chain investigator ZachXBT has put at more than $133 million and that the bank has not confirmed. The Brittany-based lender said in a statement that the incident was under control, that operations were resuming and that customer assets were not affected. It suspended some transactions as a precaution. “This incident has had no impact on (customer) assets and has only caused a delay in the execution of certain transfers,” the bank said on its website, in a translation published by Reuters . In a follow-up question-and-answer note , Credit Mutuel Arkea said the attackers went through the platform of one of its service providers and reached the bank directly. They used the bank’s own account to send transactions to other banks, which then potentially allowed them to convert the money into cryptocurrency through specialized platforms, the bank said. No customer accounts at its federations or subsidiaries were used, the bank said. It denied French press reports that the attackers got in through Fortuneo, its online banking arm, and said the Credit Mutuel Arkea hack was “a sophisticated attack from the outside,” not the result of human error. The size of the Credit Mutuel Arkea hack The bank has not given a final figure. Asked whether 118 million euros, or $133 million, had been stolen, it said it does not confirm the number and can only “validate the order of magnitude.” Part of the funds involved has been frozen and other steps are underway to recover the rest, the bank said. It added that the amounts at stake are “absolutely not” large enough to threaten its financial health or soundness. AFP reported that the bank put the attack at about 100 million euros in a provisional estimate. Earlier Wednesday, Reuters reported that the bank said its losses were lower than $133 million. “It is still too early to give a final figure,” a spokesperson told the wire service. What ZachXBT reported ZachXBT first flagged the incident on Monday without naming the victim. He wrote on his Telegram channel that an EU entity was suspected of losing more than $106 million from multiple centralized exchange accounts on Nov. 1, with the funds withdrawn as USDC and USDT. He said the funds were then swapped for ether and moved across several chains. business.description: Bitcoin Magazine House Democrats Eye Their Own Crypto Market Structure Bill With a Bigger SEC Role After Sweep House Democrats are discussing a plan to turn Rep. Maxine Waters’ Crypto Investor and Consumer Bill of Rights into their own crypto market structure bill next Congress, with ideas that include a bigger role for the SEC and a smaller one for the CFTC, Eleanor Terrett reported Wednesday. The proposal would fold in the Democratic Clarity Act provisions Waters offered in the House, which were not adopted, plus the provisions Senate Democrats were able to agree on with Republicans before September’s failed cloture vote. Terrett cited three industry sources who have spoken with Democratic staffers. Further ethics provisions restricting the crypto activities of President Donald Trump and other federal officials are also likely, she wrote. Republicans are calling it a “messaging bill.” No text for the crypto market structure bill has been released, and the details so far come from industry sources rather than from lawmakers. JUST IN: House Democrats reportedly want to revive their Clarity Act provisions in a broader crypto market structure bill next Congress, Eleanor Terrett reports. pic.twitter.com/8twokppjHz — Bitcoin Magazine (@BitcoinMagazine) November 4, 2026 The talks follow Tuesday’s Democratic sweep of Congress . Waters, the top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, is in line to take the gavel in January from Chairman French Hill, the Clarity Act’s sponsor. Bloomberg Law reported Wednesday that the new majorities give Democrats leverage over the Clarity Act, the industry’s top legislative priority, starting with tougher ethics rules aimed at Trump’s ventures. What the Waters amendment would do for crypto Waters offered the bill of rights as amendment #31 to H.R. 3633 in July 2025. The House Rules Committee blocked it 4-8 along party lines, on a motion from Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon of Pennsylvania. Making an amendment “in order” lets the full House debate and vote on it, so the result kept the package off the floor. The committee’s record lists what it would have required: 24/7 customer service, insurance or SIPC-like coverage, fiduciary and best-execution rules, anti-front-running rules, bankruptcy-remote custody with 24-hour withdrawals and monthly auditor-attested proof of reserves. It would also have sent more funding to the SEC and CFTC. The committee rejected a second Democratic amendment by the same 4-8 margin. That one, from Rep. The ethics fight it previewed later followed the bill to the Senate. business.title: Bitcoin Price Holds Near $80,000 as Democratic Sweep Sparks Short Squeeze
business.description: Bitcoin Magazine Bitcoin Price Holds Near $80,000 as Democratic Sweep Sparks Short Squeeze Bitcoin price traded near $80,000 on Wednesday afternoon, up about 3% on the day and roughly $26,000 below its price one year ago, as markets shook off election-night jitters over the Democratic sweep of Congress , according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data. Bitcoin changed hands at $80,099 at 3:12 p.m. ET, with a market cap of about $1.61 trillion and roughly $39.6 billion in trading volume over the past 24 hours. The low came in the 10 p.m. ET hour on Tuesday, as results showed Democrats taking both chambers. The high came in the 10 a.m. hour on Wednesday. That is a swing of about 7.3% from bottom to top in roughly 12 hours. The climb was a short squeeze. About $950 million in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, and bets against prices made up $560 million of that. Bitcoin positions accounted for $403 million of the total, 76% of it shorts. CryptoQuant CEO Ki Young Ju wrote on X Wednesday afternoon that $215 million in bitcoin shorts were liquidated in a single hour. JUST IN: Bitcoin surges to $81,000 pic.twitter.com/k1bGzrrzCP — Bitcoin Magazine (@BitcoinMagazine) November 4, 2026 The view among analysts is that the sell-off had already done its work. CoinShares head of research James Butterfill said the sweep was largely priced into bitcoin before the vote, leaving room for a relief rally once the uncertainty cleared. Lumida CEO Ram Ahluwalia had laid out the same path in a podcast interview the day before the election. A Democratic sweep, he said, would bring “a one and done washout, and that resets where asset prices are.” Stocks, oil and a weaker dollar Bitcoin price did not rally alone. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose about 1,500 points, or 3%, on Wednesday afternoon, while the S&P 500 climbed 1.7% and the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.8%. Apple and Microsoft touched record highs. Oil moved the most. Brent crude fell more than 9% to $93.91 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate dropped nearly 9% to $87.59 by 12:36 p.m. ET, CNBC reported, after Vice President JD Vance blamed the Republican losses on the Iran war. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote on X. That matters for bitcoin price because crude above $100 has kept inflation hot and the Federal Reserve leaning toward a December hike. The U.S. dollar index fell 0.55% to 101.32 in early trading, its lowest since Oct. 1. What comes next for bitcoin price Demand from funds has not caught up with the price. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs shed $115.6 million on Tuesday, their third straight session of outflows, with BlackRock’s IBIT losing $95 million. The three-day total comes to about $1.16 billion. Wednesday’s flows will be reported after the U.S. close. The policy picture got worse for the industry, not better. entertainment.description: CAPE TOWN, South Africa: African Philanthropy Forum (APF) closed its 2026 Conference in Cape Town on 27 October with a message that ran through nearly every session: Africa’s challenges are connected, so African giving has to be connected too. Held from 25 to 27 October under the theme Bridge the Divide; Reimagine the Future , the conference brought together philanthropists, funders, business leaders, creatives, and technologists to ask how African capital can be mobilized, how partnerships can be strengthened, and how African-led solutions can be backed with more trust and flexibility. Centered on Africa, the program also looked outward, drawing on solutions from across the Global South and asking how African philanthropy can bridge the divide. The conference opened on Sunday evening with a reception at Cape Point Vineyards, where Executive Director Mosun Layode welcomed delegates, members and acknowledged APF Board members, including Chair Gbenga Oyebode , Wale Adeosun , and Nyimpini Mabunda . Former Board Member Phuthi Mahanyele-Dabengwa urged guests to look past the continent’s challenges and toward its potential and to use the days ahead to turn conversations into partnerships. It was an evening of connection before two days of ideas at the Norval Foundation. Reimagining the Future Monday, 26 October, began with a call to build bridges across regions, languages, and funding silos. Mosun Layode and Gbenga Oyebode officially opened and welcomed all delegates to the conference. Dr. Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka , former Vice President of South Africa, spoke of education as a sacred right of every African child and of bringing young people into decision-making. In the first keynote, Gary Lubner, Founder of the This Day Foundation, described giving away 95 percent of his wealth during his lifetime and said it was easier and more joyful than holding it for heirs. Old money thinking, he argued, is a major barrier to giving, and generosity includes time and effort as well as cash. The numbers framed the challenge. Delegates heard that Africa needs about $1.3 trillion in financing each year, while philanthropy contributes $5 billion to $6 billion. The task is to use that small pool to unlock far larger sources, such as pension funds and fixed-income assets, so money reaches businesses that create jobs. sports.description: Golden State Valkyries' Gabby Williams, center, celebrates with fans along the The Embarcadero during the team's WNBA Championship parade in San Francisco, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle) Did anyone go to school? Did anyone go to work? Did anyone stop smiling? It sure didn't feel like it on a sun-splashed, joyous Wednesday afternoon, when the Bay Area showed up and showed out for their newest champions, their newest local icons. The Golden State Valkyries championship parade, like almost everything the team has done in its brief lifetime, felt flawless, unique and perfectly Bay Area. A uniting, inclusive, delightful bolt of energy. The event was a mashup of an impromptu holiday, Pride parade, women's empowerment festival, Too Short concert, Blue Wave bash and - oh yeah - a sports title celebration. "It's like a movie," said Peter Guber, the team's part owner and a successful film producer. He was looking out over a cinematic scene, as the Valkyries ferry boat pulled out of the port at Jack London Square, and began the trip from Oakland to San Francisco across the sparkling bay waters. Iconic setting. Legendary characters. Spectacular story. Everything about this team has been intentional, well thought out, from the start. And the victory celebration was no exception. It united all our disparate parts, our proud identities, our different cities. It highlighted what is uniquely us . And the day after much of the nation rejected the current regime's divisive agenda, it was a feel-good, validating celebration. Though most in the throngs that lined the Embarcadero parade route were far too young to have any memory of the 49ers first Super Bowl championship, this Valkyries team has brought a similar feeling to the Bay Area. The 49ers helped bring San Francisco out of a very dark space, created by the Milk-Moscone murders at City Hall, the Jonestown tragedy in Guyana and somber days of a debilitating recession. Joe Montana and Ronnie Lott soothed the city's soul, made people proud to say they were from San Francisco. The Valkyries were born when the city was still being vilified by conservative pundits, struggling to recover from the pandemic, serving as a national punchline. Their two years of existence have coincided with the Trump administration's vicious attacks on the LGBTQ+ community, other marginalized groups and on women's rights. Which is why their victory party wasn't just about sports. It was a celebration of who we are. All of us. And particularly a celebration of women. This was our first sports party for a professional women's team, representing the half of society shut out of sports for too long. One that used love and friendship and the fight for equity as keys to victory. This is the first women's professional team to stand on the mountaintop with the Bay Area's other sports icons. "The report was accurate," he said, "just not totally exactly detailed up." What does that mean? Well, the part of the report from Fox's Jay Glazer that included how Jennings declined to get on a FaceTime call with Shanahan and general manager John Lynch , who were hoping to seal the deal? That was wrong, Shanahan said. Or, rather, not totally exactly detailed up. "It was actually - it was J.J. FaceTiming me," Shanahan said. "… It was a good talk, but he's with good people (in Minnesota). He likes where he's at. And I thought it made sense what he said and I agreed with him." That doesn't make total sense. Jennings has six catches on 10 targets in six games with a 6-1 team that values him so little that it's willing to trade him to a 6-1 team it could be battling for the NFC's No. 1 seed. And he's enjoying that situation so much that he declined a trade to his employer for his first six NFL seasons (2020-2025) that clearly still values him? It sounds like there's more to the story, possibly having to do with the 49ers not meeting Jennings' contract extension demands last year. The Ringer founder made his case on Tuesday’s episode of “The Bill Simmons Podcast.” His argument also centered on potential expansion in Las Vegas and Seattle, which could bring billions in fees to the league’s current owners. Bill Simmons Targets Adam Silver Over NBA Schedule and Potential Expansion Fees The podcaster opened his criticism by directing it at the league office. “Listen, I don’t know how many times I’ve talked about this on the pod about the schedule and about how this, to me, is just inexcusable and semi-reprehensible that whoever is in charge of the league, which I think is Adam Silver these days, that he doesn’t care,” Simmons said . The NBA has maintained an 82-game regular season since 1967-68, apart from seasons shortened by labor disputes or other disruptions. He continued, “You’re ruining your players … and you’re hurting careers, and you’re shortening careers. This should be a 70-game season. And if you talk to literally everybody who plays basketball, all of them would say the season needs to be shorter. And if you don’t do it at this point, I just think it’s negligent. I really do. I think it’s actual negligence and greed.” The NBA has 30 franchises, and adding teams in Las Vegas and Seattle would mark its first expansion since the Charlotte Bobcats joined the league in 2004. That potential expansion is central to Simmons’ argument because of the money he expects the league’s current owners to receive. “The question for me is, you’re gonna make all this money … that’s gonna be $9.5 billion for the [Las Vegas] expansion team … They’re gonna get a second thing from Seattle, which is gonna be $7.5 (billion), something like that. … So all these owners are getting, I don’t know, $16 billion in expansion fees,” he said. Cutting 12 games from each team’s schedule would also mean fewer home dates and fewer opportunities to sell tickets and concessions. sports.title: Rece Davis: CFP rankings show ‘needs to be reimagined’ when bracket expands to 24
sports.description: Credit: ESPN If the College Football Playoff rankings show feels like a chore with a 12-team field, just imagine how it will be with 24 teams starting next season. After the heavily criticized first rankings release of the season on ESPN this week, host Rece Davis deftly avoided direct criticism of the selection committee while noting on The Pat McAfee Show that he expected significant turnover among the teams going forward. Davis is tasked with interviewing committee chair Hunter Yurachek about the list each week, and creating some semblance of a track record over the course of the season. In a follow-up conversation Wednesday on The College GameDay Podcast , Davis expressed uncertainty over the future of the rankings show. “If this continues … I don’t know that the show itself continues. I assume it will, because it’s still under the original contract,” he said. “But it will certainly feel different. It felt different when we went to 12 a couple of years ago, it’s certainly going to feel different when we go to 24.” While insider Pete Thamel confirmed that he expects the rankings show will continue under the CFP’s updated agreement with ESPN , Davis acknowledged the show could become very dry running through two-dozen teams. The longtime College GameDay host suggested the show should not air any rankings beyond 25 even once the tournament expands, and offered the idea of perhaps starting with the first team out to build suspense. “It probably needs to be reimagined,” he said. “I mean, are we really going to start … at 35? But then people are like, ‘Let’s go.’ So I think if you start at 25, [it’s], ‘OK here’s the first team out.’ Maybe you do it like that.” The show draws millions of viewers and theoretically helps the CFP selection committee hold itself accountable. However, it has become a source of tension at ESPN and in the industry. Star commentator Kirk Herbstreit bowed out from the broadcast early on , and in-house critics such as Michael Wilbon have railed against the rankings show. When the field doubles in size , ESPN could have a different issue on its hands. The show could simply become too boring or monotonous for fans. The analyst company expects inference to account for over 70 percent of computing demand by next year, adding that it's growing fastest at the edge. Why enterprises are building their own All this investment in AI infrastructure might once have come mainly for hyperscalers, but that's changing quickly. Adoption is spreading quickly beyond public cloud service providers into enterprise environments, IDC adds. They're eager to run agentic AI in-house. There are plenty of reasons for companies to own their own AI infrastructure rather than offloading it to the cloud. One of these is data control, especially in regulated sectors such as finance, healthcare, manufacturing, and the public sector that have sovereign data requirements. Another revolves around the need for predictable costing from tokens delivered on tunable in-house systems. So what should companies look for in a supplier? Delivery speed will be a powerful driver for many who are under the gun to deliver AI initiatives for the business, especially during periods of constrained memory and CPU supply. Life cycle services will also come near the top of the list, for companies that need help managing everything from the power through to the reasoning LLM models and the workloads that use them. That need for expertise is unlikely to stop; companies will undergo changes in AI strategy as they get to grips with a still-evolving technology. technology.title: Nintendo's biggest ROM chip supplier is bowing out of the business
technology.description: For years, the AI industry's insatiable demand for memory and storage has had plenty of knock-on effects on the price and availability of PC components like RAM , SSDs , and GPUs . Now those shortages are also squeezing the supply of ROM chips that power physical Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 game cartridges. Chip manufacturer Macronix announced in its third-quarter earnings report that the company's production of ROM chips "has reached its end" and that it will begin "gradually decoupling from the game industry," as reported by Taiwanese news site BigGo Finance . That could be an issue for Nintendo, which analyst David Gibson notes uses Macronix as its "main memory chip maker" for physical game cartridges. That ROM production—which has shrunk 39 percent in the last year and now represents just 5 percent of Macronix's business—is being crowded out by production of more lucrative, in-demand chips like NOR- and NAND-based memory and eMMCs, the company said. With Macronix's production capacity stuck at 25,000 12-inch wafers a month—and $1.2 billion in planned new capacity taking a year or more to spin up—less profitable ROM chips are taking up wafer space that can earn more through other types of chips. technology.title: Uranium cubes reveal why the German nuclear project failed
technology.description: During World War II, physicists on the Manhattan Project worried that the Nazi German nuclear program might achieve the first nuclear bomb before the US and its allies. That's not what transpired, but historians have debated just how close the Germans came to achieving criticality in their last attempt at building a reactor: the B8 pile. Werner Heisenberg, who led that effort, claimed that they were close and had only needed a little more uranium. But according to a paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences Nexus, that was not the case: the project simply didn't have sufficient uranium and heavy water to build a working bomb, given the design they were using. This particular research started in 2013, when University of Maryland physicist Timothy Koeth—a co-author on the new paper—received the gift of a mysterious heavy metal cube from a friend. He instantly recognized it as one of the uranium cubes used by German scientists in their unsuccessful attempt to build a working nuclear reactor. Only 14 such cubes are known to exist today. In 2019, we reported on Koeth’s quest to track down the cube’s origins, as well as several other similar cubes that had somehow found their way across the Atlantic. At the time, Koeth and his partner in the quest, then-graduate student Miriam “Mimi” Hiebert, had tracked down ten such cubes around the US. For instance, the Smithsonian Institute had a German uranium cube in storage. They tracked a third cube to Harvard University, where it was regularly passed around to students in introductory physics classes as a curiosity. Read full article Comments

technology.title: Apple turns iCloud into spy cloud, will start looking at public share links
technology.description: If you share content using public iCloud links, Apple could soon be looking over your shoulder and checking for "harmful content." The iBiz announced plans to moderate publicly accessible iCloud share links in version 27.3 of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS on a support page published on Tuesday. To clarify, this applies only to iCloud content shared via links created to be accessible to anyone, as opposed to content shared directly with other people. “Items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content,” Apple explained on the new help page without bothering to define what harmful content means. Based on the wording, it appears those checks will apply to all iCloud items shared using "Anyone with the Link," which Apple says it can also access. The company hasn't explained how the checks will work. The share-with-anyone option removes end-to-end encryption from the shared item, Apple said, even if Advanced Data Protection , Apple's optional end-to-end encryption feature for supported iCloud data, remains enabled for the account. “If you try to upload harmful content, Apple reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete the content at any time,” the help page continues, adding that the iMaker may also block or disable accounts associated with harmful content. The company also said it reserves the right to involve law enforcement when necessary, suggesting that its undefined "harmful content" category could include child sexual abuse material (CSAM), malware, and other potentially unlawful content. Without a proper definition of what it defines as harmful, however, iCloud users are essentially left at Apple’s mercy: If it chooses to continue to bend the knee to the Trump administration, for example, content deemed objectionable by the standards of political figures could end up wiped out. Apple also hasn't explained whether human moderators, automated systems, or both will be responsible for identifying and removing so-called harmful content, or whether any decisions will be left to AI, which can easily be fooled into making a bad moderation call. The scanning of such content, as mentioned above, begins with version 27.3 of Apple’s various OSes, which were released to developers in beta on Tuesday, with a general release expected in December. Apple didn’t respond to questions for this story. ®

technology.title: Hey, Siri: Plug into my app like you said you'd do way back in 2024
technology.description: As of Tuesday, developers can explore expanded Siri AI integration for their Apple platform apps through beta releases of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3. Next spring, nearly three years after announcing plans for deeper third-party Siri integration, Apple expects to begin accepting App Store submissions using the new capabilities. "This developer beta offers a sneak peek at Siri AI app intents for developers," Apple said in a developer news post . "With this early Developer Preview, your app can work directly with Siri AI, giving you a first look at new ways to reach and serve your customers." Anything is likely to be an improvement. Apple's Siri, a voice-activated assistant service, dates back to 2011 and gained limited third-party app access in 2016. In 2024, it became an interface for interacting with Apple Intelligence, its suite of generative AI features. Apple Intelligence has not been very intelligent – several advertised Siri capabilities were delayed, so much so that Apple was sued in 2025 over allegations of misleading marketing. After a shakeup of Apple's machine learning group in December 2025, Siri and Apple Intelligence received a makeover at Apple's Worldwide Developers Conference in June. "Before this year, Siri was a timer with a voice," said Roberto Gutierrez, Apple platforms staff engineer at a media company and author of the e-book On-Device Intelligence, in an email to The Register . "Weather, alarms, calls. Anything past that was a coin toss. "On the developer side, SiriKit covered a handful of domains and Shortcuts only worked if users memorized the phrase. Siri AI is the first version that understands context and can chain actions across apps. That's a real change." There is a catch, however, Gutierrez observed. Siri AI is available in a limited number of languages and regions. Support for Traditional Chinese is expected by the end of 2026, and EU availability remains a matter of negotiation – Siri AI is unavailable on iOS, iPadOS, and watchOS in the bloc as Apple works through interoperability concerns under Europe's Digital Markets Act. "Apple is working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward," the company said last month without committing to any concessions. Gutierrez said that he expects opening Siri to third-party developers will be useful to some extent. "Siri can only do what apps expose through App Intents, and SiriKit is on its way out," he said. "If your app's main actions aren't exposed, the new Siri can't see you. The bigger shift is letting Claude, Gemini and others plug in. science.title: NASA Announces X-70 Experimental Aircraft to Advance Flight Research
science.description: Generated image of NASA’s new X-70 Fractal experimental aircraft, a crewed, rapidly reconfigurable research platform for advanced aviation technologies. On Wednesday, NASA unveiled its newest experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, during the UP.Summit at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This high-performance, highly adaptable research platform is designed to accelerate the development and testing of advanced aviation technologies. The crewed X-70 features advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will allow NASA to explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight. The aircraft can also accommodate up to 2,000 pounds of experimental payloads in internal and external locations, enabling a wide range of research and flight-testing opportunities. “The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Its modular design and ability to rapidly swap internal and external payloads will keep our teams flying, learning, and moving quickly from one experiment to the next. We expect her first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years, and X-70 is just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics. This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly.” The X-70 Fractal has a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds and is designed to cruise at Mach .75, reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet, and provide an operational range exceeding about 1,726 miles (1,500 nautical miles). These capabilities will enable NASA to conduct demanding flight research across a broad range of operating conditions. “For decades, NASA Aeronautics has used X-planes to develop technologies that advance aviation,” said Laurie Grindle, director of the Aeronautics Division within NASA’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate. “It’s exciting to bring on another X-plane to accelerate and drive aeronautics research.” The X-70 joins a storied legacy of experimental aircraft that have helped establish America’s leadership in aviation. From the Bell X-1, which first broke the sound barrier in 1947, to the X-15 hypersonic research aircraft and today’s X-59 quiet supersonic demonstrator, NASA has spent decades pushing the boundaries of flight. With the X-70, NASA will expand its capacity to conduct experimental flight research, accelerate the testing of emerging technologies, and advance the next generation of American aviation. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 4, 2015: A rail-launched Super Strypi rocket carrying 13 baby satellites failed during its debut launch for the US Air Force
science.description: null On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force planned to launch an experimental rocket for small satellites from the Pacific Missile Range Facility off Barking Sands, Kauai, Hawaii. The launch didn't according to plan . For this mission, the Air Force was testing out the Super Strypi rocket . The rocket used a rail to help with the liftoff. Super Strypi left the ground, but the rocket quickly spun out of control. When it crashed, it destroyed all of the tiny satellites riding aboard the rocket. The cause? Likely a problem with the first stage motor. The mission lost 13 tiny satellites known as cubesats. Cubesats are a popular option for space missions, because they are small and cheap, and they often operate in swarms. After failing to launch this batch of cubesats, the Super Strypi program never recovered from its failure, and the Air Force never tried launching another one. The U.S. Air Force’s rail-launched Super Strypi rocket lifted off from Hawaii about 9:45 p.m. local time on Nov. 3, 2015,, roared toward the sky and failed less than a minute into the long-awaited flight. (Image credit: U.S. Air Force) Why it mattered The Super Strypi rocket was a 21st century take on a 1960s rocket. It was designed to be a modern version of the three-stage Strypi sounding rocket used for for reentry vehicle and anti-missile target tests. Its three stages, powered by Aerojet Rocketdyne solid rocket motors, was designed to reach orbit, rather than suborbital trajectories common to most sounding rockets. The U.S. Air Force hoped Super Strypi would be a new tool for quick-response launches based on national security needs. Altogether, it was designed to launch small payloads of up to 300 kilograms into space for a mere $15 million per mission . The rocket's primary payload was the ORS-4 satellite, short for Operationally Responsive Space 4, which was built for the Air Force by engineers at the University of Hawaii (who nicknamed it HiakaSat). It was designed to capture Earth imagery and monitor the environment over the course of a year. The 12 other payloads on Super Strypi included eight cubesats for NASA's Edison Demonstration of Smallsat Networks mission, and as well as four others for universities that had been added as secondary payloads. Since the Super Strypi failure, neither the Air Force or Space Force has opted to use the rocket for a new mission. The Space Force has turned instead to commercial companies for fast-turnaround launch support. In June of this year, the U.S. Space Force teamed up with Rocket Lab to launch the Victus Haze mission with just 17 hours of notice , a new record to demonstrate short-turnaround launch response.

science.title: Trump declares 'American space superiority for all eternity' in election night proclamation
science.description: null President Trump issued a declaration yesterday (Nov. 3), proclaiming space open to all humanity for exploration, and the right of American citizens to develop and settle the solar system according to United States laws. "The American Declaration of Freedom in Space," describes space as the "province of all humans" and asserts that the United States will lead humanity's expansion into the cosmos. The proclamation reiterates the administration's goals with NASA's Artemis program to return American astronauts to the moon by 2028 and eventually sending astronauts to Mars , but introduces no new funding, programs or policy directives. "Our Nation will lead the way in the exploration, development, use, and settlement of these new frontiers — forging an interplanetary civilization founded on the enduring and inalienable rights of freedom and individual liberty," the document says. Trump invoked America's "frontier spirit," highlighting Apollo 11 astronauts as the first people in history to walk on the moon's surface and robotic rovers exploring Mars as examples of U.S. leadership, and emphasized the country's flourishing commercial space sector helping ensure "American space superiority for all eternity." "The nation that leads in space will shape the future of humanity," the declaration says, and pledges that America will carry the values of faith, freedom and individual liberty into an interplanetary civilization. The proclamation also highlights the success of NASA's Artemis II mission in April, which carried four astronauts on a 10-day journey around the moon and set a record for the farthest humans have ever traveled from Earth . The follow-up to that mission, Artemis III, is scheduled to launch next summer (2027), and will test rendezvous and docking operations between NASA's Orion spacecraft and the program's two commercial lunar landers in low Earth orbit . Artemis IV will be the program's first lunar landing mission, and is targeted for 2028. A December 2025 executive order from the President reaffirmed the goal of meeting that timeline, as well as the deployment of the initial elements for a permanent lunar outpost by 2030. Trump's declaration yesterday does not establish new NASA programs, allocate additional funding or issue instructions to federal agencies. Its sweeping language, though, does echo some of the principles in the 1967 Outer Space Treaty , which guarantees freedom of exploration while prohibiting national sovereignty claims on other planets.

science.title: 'Trials and Tribble-ations' at 30: The classic 'Star Trek: Deep Space Nine' episode that brought Captains Kirk and Sisko face-to-face
science.description:
Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor. 

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.  

When "Star Trek" celebrated its 60th anniversary in September, it was a strangely muted affair. Sure, there were fan events, screenings, and even an attempt at a world record for the biggest simultaneous Vulcan salute in history , but the lack of a "Doctor Who"-style birthday episode felt like a glaring omission. It was like everyone had shown up for the party, but the organizers had forgotten to book the headline entertainment. Luckily, there were rather more fireworks for the show's 30th birthday, when both "Voyager" and "Deep Space Nine" marked the occasion in style. "Voyager" episode "Flashback" took Tuvok (Tim Russ) back to his days on the USS Excelsior bridge alongside Original Series vets Hikaru Sulu (George Takei) and Janice Rand (Grace Lee Whitney). But it was "DS9"'s "Trials and Tribble-ations" that turned out to be the more memorable voyage to "Trek" past, as Captain Benjamin Sisko (Avery Brooks) — with the help of some then-state-of-the-art digital trickery — came face-to-face with a young Captain James T. Kirk (William Shatner). While "Flashback" aired within days of "Trek"'s September 8 birthday, fans had to wait a little longer for "DS9"'s contribution to the celebrations. Showrunner Ira Steven Behr was keen to avoid disrupting the space station-set drama's story arc for a comedic diversion, meaning that "Trials and Tribble-ations" didn't debut until November 4, 1996. science.title: NASA's Swift space telescope crashes back to Earth after failed rescue attempt
science.description: null NASA's Swift space telescope has reached the end of its long and winding road. Swift fell uncontrolled to Earth today (Nov. 4), 22 years after it launched but just three months after a private spacecraft was supposed to boost it to a higher, life-extending orbit. The 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) observatory reentered Earth's atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST (1239 GMT) today over northern Sumatra, according to satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell , who cited U.S. Space Force data. The fall likely didn't make much of an impact; NASA officials predicted beforehand that most of the minibus-sized Swift would burn up as it fell, and they put the odds of any of the surviving pieces hurting anyone on Earth at just 1 in 2,100. Swift — officially known as the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer — launched to Earth orbit in November 2004 on a two-year mission to study gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the most powerful explosions in the universe . "Swift" was not an acronym but rather referred to the spacecraft's observational agility. "Swift needed to detect and locate gamma-ray bursts, communicate their position to other observatories, and then swing its telescopes around to image the burst locations before their afterglows faded out," S. Bradley Cenko, Swift's principal investigator (PI) at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, said in an Oct. 23 statement . "This typically took Swift about a minute to do." Swift didn't just observe GRBs. It also studied a variety of other cosmic bodies and phenomena, from faraway supernova explosions and feeding black holes to asteroids and comets in our own solar system. And it kept doing this long after its warranty expired — for about 20 years after, in fact. The space telescope didn't conduct its final science observation until this past Oct. 20 . (Swift underwent a name change during this stretch: In 2018, it was rechristened the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory after its first PI, who died the previous year.) "Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long," Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of NASA's Astrophysics Division, said in the same Oct. 23 statement. "In that time, Swift played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics that showed how critical rapid-response observations are to the entire community," he added. (Image credit: Katalyst Space)) Swift was incredibly productive, observing more than 2,000 GRBs and 1,400 supernovas over the course of its long scientific life. But it could have gathered even more data, had a dramatic rescue mission worked out. science.title: Toothbrush that emits electricity may more effectively prevent gum disease
science.description: A new and improved toothbrush could help avoid trips to the dentist Westend61/Alamy A toothbrush that generates electricity may more effectively fight harmful bacteria, while removing plaque, than existing products. The toothbrush uses special bristles that produce electricity as they bend, triggering the formation of molecules that damage bacterial membranes. When put to the test, it led to more than twice the reduction of plaque, gum inflammation and bleeding as conventional toothbrushes. “The concept is great,” says Nicholas Jakubovics at Newcastle University, UK, who wasn’t involved in the research. “Basically, the mechanical forces recharge the surface, so it’s really innovative. Anything that even slightly improves the way dental care works could have a benefit, because oral disease is just so widespread.” Read more How regrowing your own teeth could replace dentures and implants Oral diseases, such as tooth decay, affect nearly half the global population . Brushing regularly can help remove plaque, a sticky layer of bacteria that forms on teeth. These bacteria can produce acids that cause cavities and irritate gums, sometimes leading to tooth loss. Advertisement But even thorough brushing can leave behind bacteria deep in plaque or between teeth, allowing colonies to grow back within hours. Researchers have previously developed toothbrushes with antibacterial metal nanoparticles, including silver and zinc, embedded in their bristles , although their long-term effectiveness is uncertain. Others have designed ionic toothbrushes that use electric currents to help loosen plaque , but they are dependent on batteries. Now, Yanhui Lu at Peking University in China and her colleagues have turned to studies showing that so-called piezoelectric materials fight bacteria in infected wounds and medical implants. These generate electric charges under pressure , prompting Lu’s team to develop toothbrush bristles made from piezoelectric plastic. Laboratory tests confirmed the bristles generated electricity under pressure, particularly the thicker ones. science.title: Mars isn't dead — recent volcanic activity reveals it's just sleeping
science.description: null Scientists have long suspected that Mars is geologically "dead," but new spacecraft observations suggest the Red Planet's volcanoes are merely sleeping. That means that Olympus Mons , the extinct Martian volcano that at around 16 miles (26 kilometers) above the surrounding Martian plains is the largest mountain in the solar system , may in fact be a slumbering giant. The observations were made with the European Space Agency (ESA) mission ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) as it studied volcanic fissures along the Alba Mons region of the Red Planet. Alba Mons is in the Tharsis region of Mars, the same area that is home to Olympus Mons. While the latter is the tallest volcano in the solar system, at 374 miles (600 km) across, about the size of Arizona, the Alba Mons region is the largest volcano when considering surface area. TGO detected gas containing hydrogen chloride making its way to the surface of Mars through the Alba Mons fissures. The same gas is commonly found escaping from magmatic vents on Earth, with the compound coming from hot magma beneath the surface. Detecting it on Mars is a sign of dormant Martian volcanism. Orbital imagery had previously shown some volcanoes appear to have been active within the last few million years, and seismometers have detected the rumbling of "marsquakes," both implying the Red Planet is volcanically active. However, eruptions and lava flows have been conspicuous by their absence. "Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does," team co-leader and scientist at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences, Daniel Mège, said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "The TGO was able to find the smoking gun. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack." Evidence of dormant Martian volcanism is rising Mège and colleagues were first alerted to something strange happening on Mars when they noticed spikes of hydrogen chloride during Martian summer and on the northern hemisphere of the Red Planet. That is both a time and place at which hydrogen chloride shouldn't be detected. The gas usually peaks in the northern hemisphere during winter on Mars, disappearing in the summer. This variation is connected to the water and dust cycle on Mars. An exception to the rule occurs over volcanic fissures on the flanks of the Alba Mons volcano, in early summer. The TGO followed up on this by detecting fresh and narrow fissures, in some cases hundreds of feet long, in the Alba Mons region. A clear sign of volcanism. "It's truly amazing that it spotted a handful of molecules from a perhaps intermittent source, whilst moving continuously along its orbit to monitor the whole Martian atmosphere," Mège said. science.title: NASA Announces Ka-Band Satellite Relay Awards for Space Communications
science.description: Credit: NASA NASA selected three companies on Wednesday to perform work to develop Ka-band space relay capability concepts that are compatible with current missions in space, ensuring service continuity for existing spacecraft without requiring modifications to their onboard systems. Through this work, NASA will aim to acquire end-to-end solutions that include space, ground, launch, operations, and integration elements, as one of many customers in the commercial marketplace. The awards, under the Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships-3 Broad Agency Announcement Appendix E, are firm-fixed-price contracts that give NASA the option to provide additional funding up to the award limit to advance from initial concept development and risk reduction to an in-orbit flight demonstration. The initial period of performance runs from Nov. 4 through May 3, 2027, with additional priced options to continue work through 2029. The contract awardees with maximum potential value inclusive of all future options are: Astranis Space Technologies Corp. for $264.3 million. Global Enterprise Solutions Inc. for $340.4 million. Viasat Inc. for $460.9 million. Facilitated through the agency’s SCaN (Space Communications and Navigation) program’s Communications Services Project, this work supports NASA’s decision to gradually retire the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite fleet and adopt commercial services for future missions. In addition to the commercial capabilities currently under development by the program’s industry partners, Ka-band services are needed to support select in-orbit missions that cannot feasibly modify flight hardware or transition to non-compatible commercial services.
